newsitem.title: UK: UK Tory favourite Clarke vulnerable over Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK Tory favourite Clarke vulnerable over Europe.

text.p: For millions of British abour voters smugly watching the Conservative Party struggling to recover from its May Day election mauling, there is only one politician who could stop Labour winning the next election -- Kenneth Clarke.
The rumbustious former finance minister is his party's best parliamentary performer and one of the few senior Conservatives with the common touch.
His man-of-the-people style is backed by political substance. Clarke has been successful in a number of top posts including interior minister and health minister.

Not surprisingly Clarke is favourite with bookmakers to succeed former prime minister John Major, who announced his resignation as party leader immediately after the May 1 polls which swept him out of office, in a party election on June 10.
But the issue that helped end 18 years of Conservative rule -- ties with the European Union -- could yet stop Clarke securing his party's top job.
For Clarke is unashamedly, stubbornly and loudly pro-European and has refused to change his views in the face of huge pressure from the party's powerful "Eurosceptics".

It is widely believed that, had it not been for Clarke, the Conservatives would have abandoned their "wait-and-see" stance on a single European currency and explicitly ruled out British participation before the election.

Eurosceptics believe that could have snatched election victory for the party but Major was under no illusion that Clarke would have resigned if policy had changed, increasing an impression that his party was hopelessly split.

The only one of the five leadership contenders to come from the centre-left of the party, Clarke believes the Socialist victory in French elections and German splits over gold reserves has taken the heat out of the European issue and will not affect the leadership chase.
But he made many Eurosceptic enemies before the election who could still take their revenge in an election unlikely to be settled in the first round of voting.

Clarke, a portly 56-year-old with a fondness for brown suede shoes, traditional English ale, jazz and bird-watching, relishes confrontation and has never minced his words in tackling his anti-European critics.
Last year, he said it would be "complete folly" to rule out British participation in a single currency and "pathetic" if Britain waited to see how monetary union developed before making up its mind.
Clarke is refreshingly candid by the standards of most politicians. He is said to be popular with subordinates and to enjoy friendly relations with his Labour party opponents.
"I admire him because he stands up for what he believes in," said Peter Mandelson, Labour's campaign manager, in a pre-election newspaper interview.

"He has no pomposity, no arrogance about him, not like most born-to-rule Tories who go around with their noses stuck up in the air. He appears to have a disdain for personal image and presentation which I find rather attractive."
Born into a working-class family in Nottingham on July 2, 1940, Clarke earned a law degree at Cambridge University and entered parliament in 1970.
After holding a junior minister's job in the Health and Social Security Department, he was made paymaster-general with a seat in the cabinet in 1985.

After the 1987 election, Clarke was made a minister for trade and industry. This was followed by a rapid rise to Health Secretary in 1988, Education Secretary in 1990 and Home Secretary (interior minister) after the 1992 general election.
High-profile confrontations with health workers, teachers and police leaders in his various ministerial posts gave Clarke the image of a political bruiser.
He became Chancellor of the Exchequer in May 1993 when Major sacked his predecessor Norman Lamont.

At the Treasury, Clarke earned a reputation for sound economic management, presiding over a sustained economic upturn, with remarkably low inflation by Britain's dismal historical standards and sharply falling unemployment.
The last six months of Clarke's chancellorship were marked by a disagreement with Bank of England Governor Eddie George over interest rates.
George, worried that inflation was set for a resurgence, argued repeatedly for interest rates to be raised to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent.

Clarke rejected the Bank's advice, arguing that the economic signals were mixed, but some economists suspected his motives were political -- a reluctance to saddle millions of home-owners with dearer mortgages in the run-up to the election.

The Chancellor's characteristically robust response was that he had never hesitated to make unpopular decisions when he thought it necessary and would do so again. "I am not going to take any risks with the recovery," he said.

However, just days after the election, interest rates were indeed raised to 6.25 percent by Clarke's successor in the Treasury, Labour's Gordon Brown, who will benefit from what Clarke calls the best economic performance in a generation.
